content: When a recommendation is expected to have the greatest impact in a specific setting, a strong recommendation is deemed appropriate. If the recommendation is likely to improve access to an intervention for those most in need, it is also likely to receive strong support. The higher the acceptability of the recommendation among stakeholders, the more likely it is to be strongly endorsed. Factors such as values, preferences, acceptability, resource implications, and feasibility of implementation are all considered when formulating recommendations. During the guideline development meeting, the chairs and methodologists worked to achieve consensus. After discussing all comments and questions from the group members, the chair asked for agreement on the recommendations to document consensus. Although voting was not required, the group had previously agreed that a two-thirds majority would be necessary for a decision. Ultimately, all group members agreed with the recommendations. For each recommendation, the group also evaluated implementation needs and identified areas requiring further research. Before finalization, the draft guidelines were reviewed and revised by both the Guidelines Development Group and an external review group. In line with WHO policy, all external contributors, including members of the Guidelines Development Group and the External Review Group, completed a declaration of interest form. This included information on consulting roles, advisory panels, research support, and financial investments. The WHO Steering Committee reviewed these declarations to assess potential conflicts of interest and agreed on an approach to manage them. At the meeting, declarations of interest were reported according to WHO standards. Individuals with significant financial ties to pharmaceutical companies or those who had received substantial honoraria were considered to have a conflict of interest if it related to the guideline topic. Their participation was classified as restricted. For example, Jason Grebely's participation was restricted for the topic of point-of-care HCV RNA viral load assays. He contributed technical expertise in reviewing evidence summaries but was excluded from voting and formulating recommendations. The declarations of interest for members of the External Review Group were also reviewed, and no cases required exclusion from the review process. Any identified conflicts of interest were considered when interpreting comments from external reviewers. However, external reviewers could not make changes to the recommendations. The updated guidelines will be disseminated electronically via the WHO website and shared with regional and country offices, as well as ministries of health, through webinars, print publications, and policy briefs. Dissemination will also be supported by publishing systematic reviews and evidence in peer-reviewed journals. Successful implementation of the recommendations will depend on their integration into regional and national strategies. WHO monitors the number of HCV-infected adults, adolescents, and children who have been treated. The guidelines will be updated based on new evidence and country implementation experiences, with technical updates provided as needed. For the treatment of chronic hepatitis C in adults, adolescents, and children aged three years and older, the guidelines recommend the use of pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens. These regimens are effective across all six major HCV genotypes, achieving sustained virological response (SVR) rates of over 85%. The recommended regimens include sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. Treatment duration varies by regimen and patient characteristics, such as the presence of cirrhosis or prior treatment experience. For most patients without cirrhosis, treatment lasts 8–12 weeks. In settings with minimal genotype 3 infection, non-pangenotypic regimens like sofosbuvir/ledipasvir may also be considered. The introduction of short-course, oral, curative DAA regimens has revolutionized HCV treatment in adults, offering high efficacy and minimal side effects compared to older interferon-based therapies. However, until recently, there was limited focus on addressing HCV in children and adolescents, and no DAA regimens were approved for pediatric use. The predominant mode of HCV transmission in children is mother-to-child transmission, while older children and adolescents may acquire the infection through unsafe injections or poor infection control, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term complications. Since 2018, the high cure rates observed in adults with pangenotypic DAA regimens have been replicated in adolescents and children, leading to regulatory approvals by the FDA and EMA. For adolescents, regimens such as glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir were approved in 2020–2021. For children aged three years and older, sofosbuvir/ledipasvir was approved in 2019, followed by glecaprevir/pibrentasvir and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir in 2021. However, the sofosbuvir/daclatasvir regimen, widely used in LMICs due to its low cost and availability, lacks regulatory approval for pediatric use. The WHO recommends aligning DAA regimens across adults, adolescents, and children to simplify procurement, promote access, and support global HCV elimination efforts. A systematic review and meta-analysis commissioned by WHO evaluated the efficacy and safety of key DAA regimens in adolescents and children. The review included 49 studies, reporting high SVR rates (≥95%) across all age groups and regimens. Adverse events were generally mild, and treatment discontinuations were rare. However, younger children experienced more challenges with treatment adherence due to poor palatability of some oral formulations. The Guidelines Development Group strongly recommends treating all adolescents and children aged six years and older with chronic HCV infection, regardless of disease stage, based on high to moderate certainty of evidence. For children aged three to five years, a conditional recommendation is made due to very low certainty of evidence. Early treatment offers several benefits, including preventing disease progression, reducing transmission, and improving quality of life. Treatment is highly effective and safe, with SVR rates of ≥95% for key pangenotypic regimens. Serious adverse events and treatment discontinuations are uncommon, although younger children may face more challenges with adherence. The WHO also emphasizes the importance of expanding access to HCV treatment for children in LMICs. The use of existing adult formulations, such as sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, could be an effective way to achieve this goal. Pharmacokinetic studies support the use of these regimens in children, and further studies are planned to validate optimal dosing for regulatory approval and country adoption.
